  folds <- km$cluster
  metrics <- data.frame(fold = 1:n_folds, AUC = NA, deviance = NA)
  for (f in 1:n_folds) {
    train <- occ_env[folds != f, ]
    test <- occ_env[folds == f, ]
    model <- gbm(presence ~ ., data = train[, !names(train) %in% c('lon','lat')],
      distribution = 'bernoulli', n.trees = 1000, interaction.depth = tc,
      shrinkage = lr, bag.fraction = 0.75)
    best_trees <- gbm.perf(model, method = 'cv')
    pred <- predict(model, test[, !names(test) %in% c('lon','lat')], n.trees = best_trees, type = 'response')
    metrics[f, 'AUC'] <- pROC::auc(test$presence, pred)
    metrics[f, 'deviance'] <- -2 * sum(test$presence * log(pmax(pred, 1e-10)) + 
      (1 - test$presence) * log(pmax(1 - pred, 1e-10)))
  }
  colMeans(metrics[, c('AUC','deviance')])
}
```

Sampling bias (more records near roads/cities) is the most pervasive problem in presence-only SDM. A bias file — a raster representing relative sampling effort — can be incorporated into MaxEnt's background sampling. MaxEnt then models the RATIO of presence density to background density, canceling out sampling bias.

[CONTEXT]
Sampling bias (more records near roads/cities) is the most pervasive problem in presence-only SDM. A bias file — a raster representing relative sampling effort — can be incorporated into MaxEnt's background sampling. MaxEnt then models the RATIO of presence density to background density, canceling out sampling bias.

[REASONING]
STEP 1 — The presence-only bias problem: GBIF records cluster near roads, cities, protected areas. Without correction, MaxEnt models sampling intensity as habitat suitability — predicting high suitability near cities for ANY species. 

STEP 2 — Target-group background: Sample background points from the same biased distribution as occurrences. If both presences and backgrounds are biased toward roads, the model learns what distinguishes presences from backgrounds BEYOND roads. 

STEP 3 — Bias file construction: (1) Kernel density of ALL GBIF records (all species) in study area. High density = high sampling effort. (2) Alternative: distance to roads, distance to cities, population density as proxies. 

STEP 4 — How MaxEnt uses it: Probability of selecting background point s ∝ bias(s). This is importance sampling from the biased distribution. The model then fits: q(s) = prior(s) × exp(Σλ_i f_i(s)) / Z, where prior(s) ∝ bias(s). 

STEP 5 — Effect: Without bias file, MaxEnt confounds habitat suitability with accessibility. With bias file, model learns habitat features that distinguish presence from background WITHIN biased regions. Bias correction is most important when sampling bias correlates with environment (e.g., roads follow valleys). 

STEP 6 — Validation: Compare model with vs without bias file. Without bias file, predictions near cities are inflated. With bias file, predictions are more ecologically plausible (species mapped to habitat, not roads).

[CODE]

library(dismo)
library(raster)
library(MASS)

# Occurrence data
occ <- read.csv('occurrences.csv')
coords <- occ[, c('lon', 'lat')]

# ALL GBIF records in study area (for bias estimation)
all_records <- read.csv('all_gbif_records.csv')
all_coords <- all_records[, c('lon', 'lat')]

# 1. Kernel density of all records = sampling bias surface
bias_raster <- raster(extent(env_stack), resolution = 0.01)
bias_density <- kde2d(
  all_coords$lon, all_coords$lat,
  n = c(ncol(bias_raster), nrow(bias_raster)),
  lims = c(
    extent(bias_raster)@xmin, extent(bias_raster)@xmax,
    extent(bias_raster)@ymin, extent(bias_raster)@ymax
  )
)
bias_raster <- raster(bias_density)
bias_raster <- bias_raster / max(values(bias_raster), na.rm = TRUE)

# 2. Sample background weighted by bias
bg <- randomPoints(
  bias_raster,
  n = 10000,
  prob = TRUE  # sample proportional to bias value
)

# 3. MaxEnt with bias file
maxent_model <- maxent(
  env_stack,
  p = coords,
  a = bg,
  removeDuplicates = TRUE
)

# 4. Prediction
pred_biased <- predict(maxent_model, env_stack)

# 5. For comparison: unbiased background (uniform sampling)
bg_uniform <- randomPoints(env_stack, 10000)
maxent_unbiased <- maxent(env_stack, coords, bg_uniform)
pred_unbiased <- predict(maxent_unbiased, env_stack)

# Compare predictions
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(pred_biased, main = 'With bias correction')
plot(pred_unbiased, main = 'Without bias correction')

# Difference map
bias_correction_effect <- pred_biased - pred_unbiased
plot(bias_correction_effect, 
     main = 'Effect of bias correction\n(blue = reduced, red = increased)')

library(vegan)

simper_bootstrap <- function(community, groups, nboot = 1000) {
  simper_result <- simper(community, groups)
  boot_contributions <- list()
  for (b in 1:nboot) {
    boot_indices <- unlist(lapply(unique(groups), function(g) {
      sample(which(groups == g), replace = TRUE)
    }))
    boot_simper <- simper(community[boot_indices, ], groups[boot_indices])
    boot_contributions[[b]] <- boot_simper[[1]]$average
  }
  ci_lower <- apply(do.call(rbind, boot_contributions), 2, quantile, 0.025)
  ci_upper <- apply(do.call(rbind, boot_contributions), 2, quantile, 0.975)
  reliable <- (ci_lower > 0)
  list(simper = simper_result, ci_lower = ci_lower, ci_upper = ci_upper, reliable = reliable)
}
```

ensemble_of_opportunity <- function(predictions_list, weights = NULL) {
  standardized <- lapply(predictions_list, function(p) (p - min(p[], na.rm = TRUE)) / 
    (max(p[], na.rm = TRUE) - min(p[], na.rm = TRUE)))
  p_stack <- stack(standardized)
  if (is.null(weights)) weights <- rep(1, length(standardized))
  weights <- weights / sum(weights)
  ensemble_mean <- weighted.mean(p_stack, weights, na.rm = TRUE)
  ensemble_sd <- calc(p_stack, sd, na.rm = TRUE)
  correlation_matrix <- layerStats(p_stack, 'pearson', na.rm = TRUE)
  list(mean = ensemble_mean, uncertainty = ensemble_sd, correlations = correlation_matrix)
}

library(INLA)
library(INLAspacetime)

barrier_spde_sdm <- function(occ, env, coastline) {
  bnd <- inla.nonconvex.hull(as.matrix(occ[, c('lon','lat')]))
  mesh <- inla.mesh.2d(boundary = bnd, max.edge = c(0.3, 1), cutoff = 0.1)
  barrier_triangles <- inla.barrier.polygon(mesh, coastline)
  barrier_model <- inla.barrier.pcmatern(mesh, barrier.triangles = barrier_triangles,
    prior.range = c(1, 0.01), prior.sigma = c(1, 0.01))
  spde <- inla.spde2.pcmatern(mesh, prior.range = c(1, 0.01), prior.sigma = c(1, 0.01))
  A <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh, loc = as.matrix(occ[, c('lon','lat')]))
  idx <- inla.spde.make.index('spatial', n.spde = mesh$n)
  stack <- inla.stack(data = list(occ = occ$presence),
    A = list(A, 1), effects = list(spatial = idx, data.frame(intercept = 1, occ[, names(env)])))
  result <- inla(occ ~ -1 + intercept + bio1 + f(spatial, model = barrier_model),
    data = inla.stack.data(stack), family = 'binomial')
  list(mesh = mesh, barrier = barrier_model, result = result)
}
```

[REASONING]
Stacked species distribution models build species richness maps by fitting individual SDMs for each species and summing suitability scores across species. The ecological rationale is that community patterns emerge from individual species' environmental responses, and stacking preserves species-specific relationships lost in direct richness modeling. A key assumption is species respond independently to environment, ignoring biotic interactions that limit local coexistence. The overprediction bias (predicting more species than co-occur) arises because stacking ignores competition, though the pattern often matches the general shape of richness gradients. Comparing stacked versus direct richness predictions reveals whether environmental filtering or assembly rules better explain community structure. Endemism maps from stacked SDMs identify areas with many range-restricted species, providing conservation priorities beyond species richness alone.

import numpy as np
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier

def stack_sdms(Y, X):
    '''Stack individual SDMs to estimate species richness.'''
    n_sites, n_spp = Y.shape
    probs = np.zeros((n_sites, n_spp))
    
    for s in range(n_spp):
        rf = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=200, class_weight='balanced')
        rf.fit(X, Y[:, s])
        probs[:, s] = rf.predict_proba(X)[:, 1]
    
    richness = probs.sum(axis=1)
    range_size = (probs > 0.5).sum(axis=0)
    endemism = probs @ (1.0/(range_size+1))
    
    return {'richness': richness, 'endemism': endemism, 'probs': probs}
```

rao_quadratic_entropy <- function(community, trait_distance_matrix) {
  n_species <- ncol(community)
  p <- sweep(community, 1, rowSums(community), '/')
  Q <- sapply(1:nrow(p), function(i) {
    sum(outer(p[i,], p[i,]) * as.matrix(trait_distance_matrix))
  })
  list(Q = Q, mean = mean(Q))
}

The key ecological problem is predicting aggregate patterns like species-area relationships (SARs) and species abundance distributions (SADs) without specifying detailed mechanistic processes. This paper introduces the maximum information entropy (MaxEnt) principle as a foundational framework for ecological theory, particularly in macroecology. The key ecological problem is predicting aggregate patterns like species-area relationships (SARs) and species abundance distributions (SADs) without specifying detailed mechanistic processes. The authors hypothesize that MaxEnt, a method of statistical inference, can accurately predict these patterns by finding the probability distribution that maximizes entropy subject to constraints from empirical data (e.g., total abundance, total energy). The methodology involves applying MaxEnt to derive predicted distributions and comparing them to observed macroecological patterns, with mismatches used to infer underlying mechanisms.

[REASONING]
Step 1: Identify the core ecological challenge—predicting macroecological patterns (SARs, SADs) from minimal information.  
- WHAT: The goal is to predict how species richness scales with area (SAR) and how individuals are distributed among species (SAD) without detailed mechanistic models.  
- WHY: Traditional mechanistic models require many parameters and assumptions; a simpler, general framework is needed for broad-scale patterns.  
- HOW: Use MaxEnt, which selects the probability distribution with maximum entropy (least biased) given known constraints (e.g., total individuals, total species).  
- ASSUMPTIONS: The system is at equilibrium, and constraints are sufficient to capture key ecological structure. Implication: Predictions may fail if constraints are incomplete or system is not at equilibrium.

Step 2: Formulate the MaxEnt optimization problem for ecology.  
- WHAT: Define the probability distribution p_i (e.g., probability a randomly selected individual belongs to species i) that maximizes Shannon entropy H = -Σ p_i ln(p_i).  
- WHY: Shannon entropy measures uncertainty; maximizing it yields the least biased distribution consistent with constraints.  
- HOW: Apply Lagrange multipliers to enforce constraints (e.g., Σ p_i = 1, Σ p_i * E_i = total energy, where E_i is energy use per individual).  
- ASSUMPTIONS: Constraints are linear and known exactly. Implication: If constraints are nonlinear or uncertain, MaxEnt may produce biased predictions.

Step 3: Derive the species abundance distribution (SAD) using MaxEnt.  
- WHAT: Predict the probability that a species has abundance n (number of individuals).  
- WHY: SAD is a fundamental pattern linking species richness and evenness.  
- HOW: With constraints on total individuals (N) and total species (S), MaxEnt yields a log-series distribution (for fixed N, S) or a more general distribution with additional constraints (e.g., total metabolic energy).  
- ASSUMPTIONS: Individuals are indistinguishable except for species identity; no spatial structure. Implication: Predicts a canonical distribution that may not match real SADs if spatial aggregation or niche differences matter.

Step 4: Derive the species-area relationship (SAR) using MaxEnt.  
- WHAT: Predict how species richness increases with sampled area.  
- WHY: SAR is a key pattern for biodiversity conservation and scaling.  
- HOW: Apply MaxEnt to the spatial distribution of individuals, with constraints on total abundance and spatial autocorrelation (e.g., using a spatial entropy measure). This yields a power-law or logarithmic SAR depending on constraints.  
- ASSUMPTIONS: Individuals are randomly distributed in space (no clustering). Implication: Predicts a steeper SAR than observed if species are aggregated.

Step 5: Compare predictions to data and interpret mismatches.  
- WHAT: Test MaxEnt predictions against empirical SARs and SADs from real ecosystems.  
- WHY: Mismatches reveal missing constraints or mechanisms (e.g., dispersal limitation, niche partitioning).  
- HOW: Calculate the difference between predicted and observed patterns; if large, add new constraints (e.g., spatial clustering, metabolic scaling) and re-apply MaxEnt.  
- ASSUMPTIONS: The true distribution is the one with maximum entropy given all relevant constraints. Implication: Mismatches guide discovery of ecological mechanisms.

Step 6: Extend MaxEnt to include dynamics and multiple scales.  
- WHAT: Apply MaxEnt to predict temporal patterns (e.g., species turnover) and cross-scale patterns (e.g., abundance across habitats).  
- WHY: Ecology needs a unified theory spanning space, time, and organizational levels.  
- HOW: Use time-dependent constraints (e.g., colonization-extinction rates) or hierarchical constraints (e.g., regional vs. local species pools).  
- ASSUMPTIONS: The principle of maximum entropy holds for non-equilibrium systems if constraints are time-averaged. Implication: May require careful definition of constraints for dynamic systems.

import numpy as np
from scipy.optimize import minimize
from scipy.special import logsumexp

# Simulate ecological data: total individuals N, total species S, total metabolic energy E
np.random.seed(42)
N = 1000  # total individuals
S = 50    # total species
E = 5000  # total metabolic energy (arbitrary units)

# Simulate observed species abundances (for comparison)
observed_abundances = np.random.lognormal(mean=2, sigma=1, size=S)
observed_abundances = observed_abundances / observed_abundances.sum() * N

# Step 1: Define MaxEnt objective (negative entropy) for minimization
def neg_entropy(p):
    # p is a vector of probabilities (species relative abundances)
    p = np.clip(p, 1e-12, 1)  # avoid log(0)
    return np.sum(p * np.log(p))

# Step 2: Define constraints
# Constraint 1: sum(p) = 1
# Constraint 2: sum(p * energy_i) = E/N (average energy per individual)
# Assume each species i has energy use proportional to its abundance (simplified)
energy_per_individual = np.random.uniform(0.5, 1.5, size=S)  # per individual energy
# Total energy constraint: sum(p_i * energy_i) = E/N
target_avg_energy = E / N

# Step 3: Use Lagrange multipliers to find MaxEnt distribution
# We'll minimize negative entropy subject to constraints using scipy
def objective(lambdas):
    # lambdas[0] for normalization, lambdas[1] for energy constraint
    # Unnormalized probabilities: exp(-lambda0 - lambda1 * energy_i)
    log_unnorm = -lambdas[0] - lambdas[1] * energy_per_individual
    log_Z = logsumexp(log_unnorm)  # log partition function
    p = np.exp(log_unnorm - log_Z)
    # Negative entropy
    return neg_entropy(p)

# Constraint functions (should be zero at optimum)
def constraint_normalization(lambdas):
    log_unnorm = -lambdas[0] - lambdas[1] * energy_per_individual
    log_Z = logsumexp(log_unnorm)
    p = np.exp(log_unnorm - log_Z)
    return np.sum(p) - 1.0

def constraint_energy(lambdas):
    log_unnorm = -lambdas[0] - lambdas[1] * energy_per_individual
    log_Z = logsumexp(log_unnorm)
    p = np.exp(log_unnorm - log_Z)
    return np.sum(p * energy_per_individual) - target_avg_energy

# Initial guess for Lagrange multipliers
lambdas0 = [0.0, 0.0]

# Use SLSQP to enforce constraints
cons = [{'type': 'eq', 'fun': constraint_normalization},
        {'type': 'eq', 'fun': constraint_energy}]
result = minimize(objective, lambdas0, method='SLSQP', constraints=cons)

# Extract predicted probabilities
lambdas_opt = result.x
log_unnorm = -lambdas_opt[0] - lambdas_opt[1] * energy_per_individual
log_Z = logsumexp(log_unnorm)
predicted_p = np.exp(log_unnorm - log_Z)
predicted_abundances = predicted_p * N

# Compare predicted vs observed (e.g., using chi-squared or KL divergence)
print("Predicted abundances (first 5):", predicted_abundances[:5])
print("Observed abundances (first 5):", observed_abundances[:5])
print("MaxEnt entropy:", -neg_entropy(predicted_p))

library(gbm)

brt_spatial_cv <- function(occ_env, n_folds = 5, tc = 3, lr = 0.005) {
  km <- kmeans(occ_env[, c('lon','lat')], centers = n_folds)
  folds <- km$cluster
  metrics <- data.frame(fold = 1:n_folds, AUC = NA, deviance = NA)
  for (f in 1:n_folds) {
    train <- occ_env[folds != f, ]
    test <- occ_env[folds == f, ]
    model <- gbm(presence ~ ., data = train[, !names(train) %in% c('lon','lat')],
      distribution = 'bernoulli', n.trees = 1000, interaction.depth = tc,
      shrinkage = lr, bag.fraction = 0.75)
    best_trees <- gbm.perf(model, method = 'cv')
    pred <- predict(model, test[, !names(test) %in% c('lon','lat')], n.trees = best_trees, type = 'response')
    metrics[f, 'AUC'] <- pROC::auc(test$presence, pred)
    metrics[f, 'deviance'] <- -2 * sum(test$presence * log(pmax(pred, 1e-10)) + 
      (1 - test$presence) * log(pmax(1 - pred, 1e-10)))
  }
  colMeans(metrics[, c('AUC','deviance')])
}

from torchdiffeq import odeint

class NeuralODESDM(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, n_features, hidden_dim=64):
        super().__init__()
        self.dynamics = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(n_features + 1, hidden_dim),
            nn.Tanh(),
            nn.Linear(hidden_dim, hidden_dim),
            nn.Tanh(),
            nn.Linear(hidden_dim, 1)
        )
    
    def forward(self, t, state_and_climate):
        suitability, climate = state_and_climate[..., :1], state_and_climate[..., 1:]
        dP_dt = self.dynamics(torch.cat([suitability, climate], dim=-1))
        return dP_dt
    
    def predict_range_shift(self, initial_suitability, climate_trajectory, times):
        state = torch.cat([initial_suitability, climate_trajectory[0]], dim=-1)
        trajectory = odeint(self, state, times)
        return trajectory[..., 0]
    
    def loss_fn(self, pred_trajectory, observed_occurrence):
        return nn.BCEWithLogitsLoss()(pred_trajectory, observed_occurrence)

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from scipy.stats import linregress

np.random.seed(42)
n_islands = 20

# Island characteristics
area = np.random.exponential(10, n_islands)  # km2
dist_mainland = np.random.uniform(0.5, 50, n_islands)  # km

# Orchid bee species richness
# S = c * A^z * exp(-d * distance)
c, z, d = 3, 0.3, 0.05
richness = c * area**z * np.exp(-d * dist_mainland)
richness = np.random.poisson(richness).astype(float)

# Body size (intertegular distance, mm)
body_size = np.random.normal(4.5, 0.5, n_islands)
# Island rule: small species become larger, large become smaller on islands
# (Simplified: body size on islands vs mainland expectation)
mainland_size = 4.5
body_shift = body_size - mainland_size

# Log-log SAR
logA = np.log(area)
logS = np.log(richness + 1)
slope, intercept, r_val, p_val, _ = linregress(logA, logS)
print(f'Species-area slope (z): {slope:.3f}, R^2 = {r_val**2:.3f}')

# Distance decay
r_dist, p_dist = pearsonr(dist_mainland, richness)
print(f'Distance-richness correlation: r = {r_dist:.3f}, p = {p_dist:.4f}')

# Island rule: correlation between mainland size and size shift
# (Negative = support for island rule: large get smaller, small get larger)
r_island, p_island = pearsonr(body_size, body_shift)
print(f'Island rule test: r = {r_island:.3f}, p = {p_island:.4f}')

# Partial SAR controlling for distance

resid_rich = richness - linregress(dist_mainland, richness).intercept - linregress(dist_mainland, richness).slope * dist_mainland

This 'bottom-up' conservation planning approach acknowledges that intact food webs require suitable habitat for all trophic levels. For practitioners, the community-based criteria are also more practical because they aggregate across multiple taxa, reducing the need for species-specific data. This approach aligns with the growing emphasis on ecosystem-based management in conservation planning.

depth = np.random.uniform(0.2, 2.0, n_sites)
substrate_d50 = np.random.uniform(1, 100, n_sites)  # median substrate size (mm)

# Baetid + chironomid + hydropsychid biomass (food for salmonids)
food_biomass = 50 * np.exp(-((velocity - 0.5) / 0.4)**2) + np.random.normal(0, 5, n_sites)
food_biomass = np.maximum(food_biomass, 1)
# Shannon diversity

# Create habitat suitability criteria (HSC) curves
# HSC for velocity based on food biomass
vel_bins = np.linspace(0, 1.5, 16)
vel_centers = (vel_bins[:-1] + vel_bins[1:]) / 2
hs_by_vel = []
for i in range(len(vel_bins)-1):
    idx = (velocity >= vel_bins[i]) & (velocity < vel_bins[i+1])
    if idx.sum() > 0:
        hs_by_vel.append(food_biomass[idx].mean())
    else:
        hs_by_vel.append(0)
hs_by_vel = np.array(hs_by_vel)
hsc_velocity = hs_by_vel / np.max(hs_by_vel)

print('Velocity HSC curve:')
for v, h in zip(vel_centers, hsc_velocity):
    print(f'  v={v:.2f}: HSI={h:.3f}')

# Identify optimal velocity for restoration
optimal_vel = vel_centers[np.argmax(hsc_velocity)]
print(f'\nOptimal velocity for macroinvertebrate food production: {optimal_vel:.2f} m/s')

functional_evenness <- function(traits, abundances) {
  dist_matrix <- dist(traits)
  mst <- spantree(dist_matrix)
  branches <- mst$dist
  weights <- abundances / sum(abundances)
  branch_weights <- (weights[mst$kid] + weights[mst$parent]) / 2
  EW <- branch_weights / sum(branch_weights)
  PEW <- EW / sum(EW)
  FEve <- sum(pmin(PEW, 1 / length(PEW)) - 1 / length(PEW)) / (1 - 1 / length(PEW))
  FEve
}
```

library(gbm)

brt_spatial_cv <- function(occ_env, n_folds = 5, tc = 3, lr = 0.005) {
  km <- kmeans(occ_env[, c('lon','lat')], centers = n_folds)
  folds <- km$cluster
  metrics <- data.frame(fold = 1:n_folds, AUC = NA, deviance = NA)
  for (f in 1:n_folds) {
    train <- occ_env[folds != f, ]
    test <- occ_env[folds == f, ]
    model <- gbm(presence ~ ., data = train[, !names(train) %in% c('lon','lat')],
      distribution = 'bernoulli', n.trees = 1000, interaction.depth = tc,
      shrinkage = lr, bag.fraction = 0.75)
    best_trees <- gbm.perf(model, method = 'cv')
    pred <- predict(model, test[, !names(test) %in% c('lon','lat')], n.trees = best_trees, type = 'response')
    metrics[f, 'AUC'] <- pROC::auc(test$presence, pred)
    metrics[f, 'deviance'] <- -2 * sum(test$presence * log(pmax(pred, 1e-10)) + 
      (1 - test$presence) * log(pmax(1 - pred, 1e-10)))
  }
  colMeans(metrics[, c('AUC','deviance')])
}
```

[REASONING]
NMDS is preferred over PCA/CA for ecological community data because it uses rank-order dissimilarities (typically Bray-Curtis, which handles joint absences appropriately), not Euclidean distances. This matters: two sites sharing zero individuals of a rare species should not be considered 'similar' in the same way as two sites sharing 100 individuals of that species. PERMANOVA partitions the dissimilarity matrix by environmental factors using pseudo-F ratios derived from permutations, avoiding normality assumptions. )

library(INLA)

inla_sdm <- function(occ, env, mesh_max_edge = 0.5) {
  bnd <- inla.nonconvex.hull(as.matrix(occ[, c('lon','lat')]), convex = -0.1)
  mesh <- inla.mesh.2d(
    boundary = bnd,
    max.edge = c(mesh_max_edge, mesh_max_edge * 2),
    cutoff = mesh_max_edge / 5
  )
  spde <- inla.spde2.matern(mesh, alpha = 2)
  A_est <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh, loc = as.matrix(occ[, c('lon','lat')]))
  idx <- inla.spde.make.index('spatial', n.spde = spde$n.spde)
  stack <- inla.stack(
    data = list(presence = occ$presence),
    A = list(A_est, 1),
    effects = list(spatial = idx, 
      data.frame(intercept = 1, bio1 = occ$bio1, bio12 = occ$bio12)),
    tag = 'est'
  )
  formula <- presence ~ -1 + intercept + bio1 + bio12 + f(spatial, model = spde)
  result <- inla(formula, data = inla.stack.data(stack),
    family = 'binomial', control.predictor = list(A = inla.stack.A(stack), compute = TRUE))
  list(mesh = mesh, spde = spde, result = result)
}

n_years = 10
n_species = 30

# Community assembly simulation
time_series = []

for year in range(n_years):
    stochasticity = 1 - year / n_years
    
    # Species presence
    present = np.zeros(n_species, dtype=bool)
    if year == 0:
        present[np.random.choice(n_species, 10)] = True
    else:

        trait_filter = np.exp(-((traits[:, 0] - 0.5))**2 / (0.1 + 0.4 * stochasticity))
        present = np.random.binomial(1, trait_filter * 0.6) > 0

Step 2: For each grid cell, compute the absolute difference between the two normalized suitability values. Step 3: Schoener's D = 1 - 0.5 * sum(|p1_i - p2_i|). Step 4: Also compute Hellinger distance I = sqrt(1 - sum(sqrt(p1_i * p2_i))), which is more sensitive to differences in low-suitability areas. Step 5: Use null models to test significance: randomize occurrences and recompute D to generate a null distribution. Step 6: D < null expectations indicates niche divergence; D > null indicates niche conservatism.

library(ENMTools)

schoeners_d <- function(pred1, pred2, null_reps = 100) {
  p1_norm <- pred1[] / sum(pred1[], na.rm = TRUE)
  p2_norm <- pred2[] / sum(pred2[], na.rm = TRUE)
  d_observed <- 1 - 0.5 * sum(abs(p1_norm - p2_norm), na.rm = TRUE)
  i_observed <- sqrt(1 - sum(sqrt(p1_norm * p2_norm), na.rm = TRUE))
  null_d <- replicate(null_reps, {
    cells <- sample(length(p1_norm))
    p1_shuffled <- p1_norm[cells]
    1 - 0.5 * sum(abs(p1_shuffled - p2_norm), na.rm = TRUE)
  })
  p_value <- mean(null_d >= d_observed)
  list(D = d_observed, I = i_observed, p_value = p_value, null_D = null_d)
}

Metapopulation with stochastic patch occupancy model (SPOM): SPOMs model the colonization and extinction dynamics of a species across a network of habitat patches, where patch occupancy depends on patch area and connectivity.

[CONTEXT]
Metapopulation with stochastic patch occupancy model (SPOM): SPOMs model the colonization and extinction dynamics of a species across a network of habitat patches, where patch occupancy depends on patch area and connectivity.

[REASONING]
Step 1: Delineate habitat patches in the landscape and measure their area and spatial configuration. Step 2: Incidence function model: patch i is occupied if colonized and not extinct since last survey. Step 3: Colonization probability of patch i: C_i = S_i^2 / (S_i^2 + y^2) where S_i is connectivity to occupied patches. Step 4: Connectivity: S_i = sum(occupied_j * A_j * exp(-d_ij / alpha)). Step 5: Extinction probability: E_i = min(1, e / A_i^x) where e is extinction parameter and x scales area effect. Step 6: Fit the model by maximizing the likelihood of the observed occupancy pattern across patches.

[CODE]
```python
spom_incidence_function <- function(patches, occupancy, distances, alpha_init = 1) {
  nll <- function(params) {
    alpha <- exp(params[1])
    e <- exp(params[2])
    x <- exp(params[3])
    y <- exp(params[4])
    connectivity <- sapply(1:nrow(patches), function(i) {
      sum(occupancy * patches$area * exp(-distances[i, ] / alpha))
    })
    Ci <- connectivity^2 / (connectivity^2 + y^2)
    Ei <- pmin(1, e / patches$area^x)
    ll <- sum(occupancy * log(Ci + 1e-10) + (1 - occupancy) * log(1 - Ci + 1e-10) +
              occupancy * log(1 - Ei + 1e-10) + (1 - occupancy) * log(Ei + 1e-10))
    -ll
  }
  fit <- optim(c(0, 0, 0, 0), nll, method = 'BFGS')
  list(alpha = exp(fit$par[1]), e = exp(fit$par[2]), x = exp(fit$par[3]), y = exp(fit$par[4]))
}

library(INLA)

inla_spatial_poisson <- function(count_data, env, mesh_max_edge = 0.5) {
  mesh <- inla.mesh.2d(
    loc = as.matrix(count_data[, c('lon','lat')]),
    max.edge = c(mesh_max_edge, mesh_max_edge * 2),
    cutoff = mesh_max_edge / 5
  )

  A <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh, loc = as.matrix(count_data[, c('lon','lat')]))

  stack <- inla.stack(data = list(count = count_data$count),
    A = list(A, 1),
    effects = list(spatial = idx, env = count_data[, names(env)]),
    tag = 'est'
  )
  formula <- count ~ bio1 + bio2 + elevation + f(spatial, model = spde)
  result <- inla(formula, data = inla.stack.data(stack),
    family = 'poisson', E = count_data$offset,
    control.predictor = list(A = inla.stack.A(stack), compute = TRUE))
  list(mesh = mesh, result = result)

[CONTEXT]
This study examines how unmodeled spatial inhomogeneity (overdispersion) affects confidence interval coverage for density estimates from SCR models.

[REASONING]
SCR models assume a Poisson point process for activity centers, but real populations show aggregation due to social structure or habitat heterogeneity. This work shows that while homogeneous SCR estimates of average density are robust, confidence interval coverage degrades when the intensity surface varies across realizations. Social aggregation (e.g., in felids) and small detector arrays exacerbate poor coverage. Understanding these limitations is crucial for reliable inference in real-world populations. This has direct implications for conservation decisions based on SCR density estimates.

```python
# Simulate overdispersion effects on SCR coverage
import numpy as np

n_simulations = 200
n_detectors = 40
true_density = 2.0  # individuals per unit area
area = 100

np.random.seed(36)

coverages = []
for sim in range(n_simulations):
    # Activity centers with overdispersion (clustered)
    # True intensity varies across realizations
    n_centers = np.random.poisson(true_density * area)
    
    # If overdispersed: variance > mean
    overdispersion_factor = np.random.gamma(2, 2)  # mean=4
    n_centers_over = np.random.poisson(n_centers * overdispersion_factor / 4) if sim % 2 == 0 else n_centers
    
    # Homogeneous estimator ignores clustering
    estimated_density = n_centers_over / area
    
    # 95% CI assuming Poisson
    se = np.sqrt(estimated_density / area)
    ci_lower = estimated_density - 1.96 * se
    ci_upper = estimated_density + 1.96 * se
    
    covered = ci_lower <= true_density <= ci_upper
    coverages.append(covered)

print(f'Confidence interval coverage (homogeneous model): {np.mean(coverages):.3f}')
print(f'Expected: 0.95 if no overdispersion')

This study applies joint species distribution models (JSDMs) to model multiple species simultaneously, accounting for residual correlations after environmental effects via latent variables.

[CONTEXT]
This study applies joint species distribution models (JSDMs) to model multiple species simultaneously, accounting for residual correlations after environmental effects via latent variables.

[REASONING]
Joint species distribution models represent a paradigm shift from single-species SDMs by modeling the entire community matrix as a unified statistical entity. The critical ecological insight is that species co-occurrence arises from three sources: shared environmental responses, biotic interactions, and shared missing covariates. JSDMs partition these using latent variables or a residual covariance matrix, asking whether two species co-occur more or less than expected after accounting for environment. For rare species, JSDMs borrow strength from common species through the shared covariance structure, improving parameter estimates that would be unreliable from single-species models. Residual correlations provide testable hypotheses about species interactions, bridging correlative and mechanistic ecology by suggesting which pairs warrant experimental study. The choice of dimension reduction (latent factors, factor analysis, or graphical LASSO) determines interpretability and computational cost, with variational methods enabling large-data applications.

import numpy as np
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

def jsdm_latent(Y, X, n_latent=3):
    '''Joint SDM with latent factors for residual co-occurrence.
    Y: (n_sites x n_spp) presence-absence; X: (n_sites x n_env)
    '''
    n_sites, n_spp = Y.shape
    
    # Environment-only models
    coef = np.zeros((X.shape[1], n_spp))
    for s in range(n_spp):
        m = LogisticRegression(C=1.0).fit(X, Y[:, s])
        coef[:, s] = m.coef_[0]
    
    # Residuals
    probs = 1/(1+np.exp(-X @ coef))
    resid = Y - probs
    
    # Latent factors from residual covariance
    pca = PCA(n_components=n_latent)
    L = pca.fit_transform(resid)  # site scores
    W = pca.components_.T         # species loadings
    
    # Species association matrix
    Sigma = W @ W.T
    np.fill_diagonal(Sigma, 1.0)
    
    return {'env_coef': coef, 'loadings': W,
            'correlations': Sigma, 'var_explained': pca.explained_variance_ratio_}
```

SpatialMaxEnt extends MaxEnt by incorporating spatial autocorrelation as a regularizer. Instead of treating occurrences as independent, SpatialMaxEnt adds a spatial covariance function (exponential or Matérn) to the model, penalizing predictions where nearby points disagree. [CONTEXT]
SpatialMaxEnt extends MaxEnt by incorporating spatial autocorrelation as a regularizer. Instead of treating occurrences as independent, SpatialMaxEnt adds a spatial covariance function (exponential or Matérn) to the model, penalizing predictions where nearby points disagree. This reduces overfitting to spatial clusters common in biased biodiversity data.

[REASONING]
STEP 1 — Problem: Standard MaxEnt assumes independent occurrences. But GBIF data is spatially clustered near roads, cities, research stations. MaxEnt overfits these clusters, producing 'bullseye' predictions around sampling locations rather than true habitat. 

STEP 2 — Spatial regularization: Add penalty term λ × Σ (q_i - q_j)² × w_ij where w_ij = exp(-distance(i,j)/range). Nearby points have high weight, forcing similar predictions. Far points have low weight (near zero), no constraint. This is a Gaussian Markov Random Field prior on the spatial surface. 

STEP 3 — Implementation: Add the spatial penalty to MaxEnt's loss function. The penalty is a quadratic form, so gradient computation adds O(m²) where m is number of presence points. For large datasets, use nearest-neighbor sparse penalty (only penalize k nearest neighbors per point). 

STEP 4 — Range selection: Cross-validation for spatial range parameter. Too large → oversmoothing (misses real habitat gradients). Too small → no regularization (overfit clusters). 

STEP 5 — Benefits: (1) More realistic probability surfaces (smooth, no bullseyes). (2) Better transfer to new regions (less overfitting to sampling bias). (3) Block CV scores improve significantly. 

STEP 6 — Caveat: Spatial smoothing can mask real fine-scale habitat patterns. For species with very specific microhabitats (e.g., cliff-nesting birds), spatial regularization may be inappropriate.

[CODE]

import numpy as np
from scipy.spatial.distance import cdist
from sklearn.isotonic import IsotonicRegression

class SpatialMaxent:
    def __init__(self, spatial_range=100, spatial_weight=0.1):
        self.range = spatial_range
        self.weight = spatial_weight
    
    def fit(self, presence_env, background_env, lr=0.01, epochs=500):
        X = np.vstack([presence_env, background_env])
        n_pres = len(presence_env)
        n_bg = len(background_env)
        
        # Spatial weights for presence points
        pres_coords = presence_env[:, :2]
        dists = cdist(pres_coords, pres_coords)
        W = np.exp(-dists / self.range)
        np.fill_diagonal(W, 0)
        
        # Initialize weights
        w = np.random.randn(presence_env.shape[1]) * 0.01
        
        for epoch in range(epochs):
            # Raw scores
            scores = X @ w
            pres_scores = scores[:n_pres]
            bg_scores = scores[n_pres:]
            
            # Log partition
            logZ = np.log(np.mean(np.exp(bg_scores)))
            
            # Standard MaxEnt loss
            loss = logZ - np.mean(pres_scores)
            
            # Spatial penalty: smoothness on presence scores
            spatial_penalty = 0.5 * np.sum(W * (pres_scores[:, None] - pres_scores[None, :])**2)
            loss += self.weight * spatial_penalty / n_pres
            
            # Gradient
            grad = X[:n_pres].T @ (np.exp(bg_scores) / np.sum(np.exp(bg_scores)))
            grad -= X[n_pres:].T @ (np.exp(pres_scores) / np.sum(np.exp(pres_scores)))
            
            w -= lr * grad[:len(w)]
        
        self.w = w
        return self
    
    def predict(self, env):
        scores = env @ self.w
        return np.exp(scores) / np.exp(scores).sum()
```

import numpy as np
# CLIMEX-like overwintering suitability index
def climex_ow(temp, precip, t_min=-5, t_max=35, p_min=400):
    # Simple CLIMEX-inspired overwintering suitability
    # Temperature stress: cold stress below t_min
    cold_stress = np.maximum(0, (t_min - temp) / abs(t_min))
    # Heat stress above t_max
    heat_stress = np.maximum(0, (temp - t_max) / t_max)
    # Moisture stress
    moist_stress = np.maximum(0, (p_min - precip) / p_min)
    total_stress = cold_stress + heat_stress + moist_stress
    return 1 - np.clip(total_stress, 0, 1)

# Simulate current vs future overwintering suitability
lats = np.linspace(20, 50, 100)
temp_current = 25 - 0.6 * (lats - 20) + np.random.normal(0, 1, 100)
temp_future = temp_current + 2.5  # RCP8.5 warming
precip = 800 + np.random.normal(0, 100, 100)

suit_current = climex_ow(temp_current, precip)
suit_future = climex_ow(temp_future, precip)
# Poleward shift detection
old_boundary = lats[np.argmin(np.abs(suit_current - 0.5))]
new_boundary = lats[np.argmin(np.abs(suit_future - 0.5))]
print(f"Overwintering boundary shift: {old_boundary:.1f}N -> {new_boundary:.1f}N")
```

library(ENMTools)

schoeners_d <- function(pred1, pred2, null_reps = 100) {
  p1_norm <- pred1[] / sum(pred1[], na.rm = TRUE)
  p2_norm <- pred2[] / sum(pred2[], na.rm = TRUE)
  d_observed <- 1 - 0.5 * sum(abs(p1_norm - p2_norm), na.rm = TRUE)
  i_observed <- sqrt(1 - sum(sqrt(p1_norm * p2_norm), na.rm = TRUE))
  null_d <- replicate(null_reps, {
    cells <- sample(length(p1_norm))
    p1_shuffled <- p1_norm[cells]
    1 - 0.5 * sum(abs(p1_shuffled - p2_norm), na.rm = TRUE)
  })
  p_value <- mean(null_d >= d_observed)
  list(D = d_observed, I = i_observed, p_value = p_value, null_D = null_d)
}

The ecological assumption is that available points represent the environment as sampled, not true absence, which implies the model estimates relative probability of use, not absolute probability.

Step 2: Address the challenge of applying logistic regression to such data. The key insight is that the logit of the probability of use is shifted by an offset equal to log(π_used / π_available), where π is the sampling proportion. Since this offset is unknown, the intercept is unidentifiable. The solution is to use a log-linear model (e.g., Poisson point process) or to treat the problem as a case-control design where the intercept is adjusted post-hoc. The ecological assumption is that the relative probability of use is proportional to the intensity of a spatial point process.

Step 3: Consider how to weight the data to reflect study design. In used-available analysis, the ratio of used to available points is arbitrary (e.g., 1:10 vs. 1:100). This ratio affects the intercept and thus the predicted probabilities. The correct approach is to set the available points to have a total weight equal to the area of the study region, making the model approximate an inhomogeneous Poisson process. The ecological assumption is that available points are a random sample from the study area, representing the environmental background.

Step 4: Use diagnostic tools to assess model fit and data properties. For presence-only data, one critical diagnostic is the calibration plot (observed vs. predicted frequency of use). If the model is well-calibrated, the slope should be 1. Another diagnostic is to check for spatial autocorrelation in residuals, which can indicate missing covariates or inappropriate scale. The ecological assumption is that residuals are independent after accounting for environmental predictors, which may fail if animals exhibit social behavior or habitat selection at multiple scales.

Step 5: Apply the method in a manner that reflects the study design. For example, if animals were tracked with GPS collars, the used points are a time series with autocorrelation. Ignoring this can inflate sample size and lead to overconfident inference. The solution is to subsample or use a mixed model with random effects for individual animals. The ecological assumption is that each location is an independent sample of habitat selection, which is violated if animals revisit the same areas.

Step 6: Compare results from different applications of the same method to the same dataset. The paper shows that using logistic regression with a 1:1 ratio vs. 1:10 ratio vs. weighted regression can produce different coefficient estimates and predictions. The correct approach depends on whether the goal is to estimate relative probability of use (which requires weighting) or to rank habitat suitability (which may be robust to ratio). The ecological implication is that model interpretation must be tied to the sampling design.

model_unweighted.fit(X, y)

weight_avail = area / n_avail  # each available point represents area/n_avail km^2

                                np.full(n_avail, weight_avail)])

plt.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], 'k--', label='Perfect calibration')

HMSC is a Bayesian joint species distribution model (JSDM) framework. Models entire species communities simultaneously, accounting for: environmental filtering, species associations (residual co-occurrence), phylogenetic relatedness, and spatial autocorrelation. Uses latent factor approach for computational tractability with hundreds of species.

[REASONING]
STEP 1 — Why joint: Species don't occur independently — they compete, facilitate, share habitat preferences. Single-species SDMs ignore these interactions. JSDM models all species together, decomposing co-occurrence into environmental (shared habitat) and residual (biotic interactions + unmeasured environment). 

STEP 2 — Latent factor model: For S species and latent factors K (K << S), species loadings Λ (S×K) encode how each species responds to unmeasured gradients. The residual covariance Σ = ΛΛ' + diag(σ²) is low-rank plus diagonal. This is O(SK²) instead of O(S³). 

STEP 3 — Fixed effects: Each species has its own environmental responses β_s. Phylogenetic signal in β tested by correlating species traits (not just taxonomy). 

STEP 4 — Spatial structure: Random effect at sampling units captures site-level variation not explained by environment. Can be spatially structured (gp) or unstructured (iid).

STEP 5 — MCMC: Gibbs sampling with adaptive Metropolis. 5000 iterations, burn-in 2500, thin by 10. Convergence via Gelman-Rubin R-hat < 1.1.

STEP 6 — Interpretation: Variance partitioning — what fraction of species occurrence is explained by environment vs. spatial vs. species associations? Species association matrix A = sign(ΛΛ') shows which species pairs co-occur more/less than environment predicts.

Develops a computationally efficient species distribution model using cumulant-based approximation applied to gamma-divergence loss, achieving Maxent-comparable accuracy with dramatically reduced computation by proving Maxent equals LDA under normality.

[CONTEXT]
Develops a computationally efficient species distribution model using cumulant-based approximation applied to gamma-divergence loss, achieving Maxent-comparable accuracy with dramatically reduced computation by proving Maxent equals LDA under normality.

[REASONING]
The computational bottleneck of Maxent and other presence-background SDMs becomes prohibitive at continental scales with high-resolution environmental layers, yet the standard approach of random background subsampling discards potentially valuable environmental information. The cumulant-based approximation (CBA) elegantly bypasses this by showing that Maxent's maximum entropy formulation is mathematically equivalent to Fisher Linear Discriminant Analysis when environmental variables follow a multivariate normal distribution, enabling closed-form estimation. This theoretical bridge between information theory and classical statistics is not just computationally convenient but ecologically illuminating: it reveals that presence-background modeling fundamentally estimates the ratio of conditional to marginal densities, a problem that LDA solves analytically. The sequential L1-penalized variable selection embedded in the approach addresses the common ecological problem of multicollinear predictors by automatically retaining only the most discriminative variables, producing simpler and more interpretable models. For conservation applications with limited computational resources, CBA makes high-resolution SDM feasible where Maxent would be impractical.

[CODE]
```python
import numpy as np
from scipy.linalg import sqrtm

def cumulant_based_sdm(X_background, X_presence, lambda_l1=0.01):
    """
    Cumulant-based approximation for species distribution modeling.
    Equivalent to Maxent under normality assumption.
    """
    mu_b = X_background.mean(axis=0)
    mu_p = X_presence.mean(axis=0)
    Sigma_b = np.cov(X_background, rowvar=False)
    
    # LDA solution
    diff = mu_p - mu_b
    Sigma_b_inv = np.linalg.inv(Sigma_b + lambda_l1 * np.eye(Sigma_b.shape[0]))
    beta = Sigma_b_inv @ diff
    
    # Sequential L1-penalized variable selection
    n_vars = len(beta)
    selected = np.zeros(n_vars, dtype=bool)
    for _ in range(n_vars):
        candidate_scores = []
        for j in range(n_vars):
            if not selected[j]:
                sel_temp = selected.copy()
                sel_temp[j] = True
                score = np.abs(beta[sel_temp]).sum()
                candidate_scores.append((score, j))
        best_score, best_j = max(candidate_scores)
        selected[best_j] = True
    
    # Habitat suitability score
    def predict(X_new):
        logit = X_new @ beta + 0.5 * (mu_b @ Sigma_b_inv @ mu_b - mu_p @ Sigma_b_inv @ mu_p)
        return 1 / (1 + np.exp(-logit))
    
    return predict, selected

# Example with simulated data
np.random.seed(42)
X_bg = np.random.multivariate_normal([0, 0, 0], np.eye(3), 10000)
X_pr = np.random.multivariate_normal([1.0, 0.5, -0.3], np.eye(3), 500)
predict_fn, sel_vars = cumulant_based_sdm(X_bg, X_pr)
print(f'Selected variables: {np.where(sel_vars)[0]}')
```

Incidence Function Models (IFM, Hanski 1994) model species occurrence as a balance between colonization and extinction in fragmented landscapes. Unlike correlative SDMs, IFM explicitly models spatial connectivity between patches — a patch's colonization probability depends on distances to and sizes of occupied patches. [CONTEXT]
Incidence Function Models (IFM, Hanski 1994) model species occurrence as a balance between colonization and extinction in fragmented landscapes. Unlike correlative SDMs, IFM explicitly models spatial connectivity between patches — a patch's colonization probability depends on distances to and sizes of occupied patches. Ideal for fragmented habitats.

[REASONING]
STEP 1 — Patch occupancy as dynamic equilibrium: In fragmented landscapes, each habitat patch is either occupied (1) or empty (0). Patch i has area A_i (larger → lower extinction) and connectivity S_i (more connected → higher colonization). 

STEP 2 — Extinction probability: E_i = min(1, e / A_i^x), where e sets baseline extinction risk and x controls area sensitivity. Small patches have higher extinction risk (Allee effects, demographic stochasticity). 

STEP 3 — Connectivity: S_i = Σ_j p_j × A_j^b × exp(-α × d_ij), summed over all occupied patches j. p_j = 1 if occupied, 0 if empty. A_j = area (emigrant source strength). α = 1/average dispersal distance. b = scaling of emigration with area. 

STEP 4 — Colonization probability: C_i = S_i² / (S_i² + y²), where y is a scaling parameter. This is sigmoidal — low connectivity → low colonization; high connectivity → saturates at 1. 

STEP 5 — Equilibrium occupancy: J_i = C_i / (C_i + E_i - C_i × E_i) (from Markov chain stationary distribution). This is the probability patch i is occupied at steady state. 

STEP 6 — Fitting: IFMs are fitted via maximum likelihood on snapshot data (occupancy status + patch characteristics). The likelihood is product over patches of J_i^o_i × (1-J_i)^(1-o_i), where o_i is observed occupancy.

[CODE]
```r
library(MetaLandSim)

# Patch data
patches <- read.csv('patches.csv')
# Columns: patch_id, area, x, y, occupied

# Distance matrix
dist_matrix <- as.matrix(dist(patches[, c('x', 'y')]))

# Incidence Function Model
IFM_fit <- function(params, patches, dist_matrix) {
  e <- params[1]  # extinction baseline
  x <- params[2]  # area sensitivity
  y <- params[3]  # colonization scaling
  alpha <- params[4]  # 1/dispersal distance
  b <- params[5]  # emigration scaling
  
  n <- nrow(patches)
  A <- patches$area
  occ <- patches$occupied
  
  # Connectivity for each patch
  S <- rep(0, n)
  for (i in 1:n) {
    S[i] <- sum(occ * A^b * exp(-alpha * dist_matrix[i, ]))
  }
  
  # Extinction probability
  E <- pmin(1, e / A^x)
  
  # Colonization probability
  C <- S^2 / (S^2 + y^2)
  
  # Equilibrium occupancy probability
  J <- C / (C + E - C * E)
  J[C == 0 & E == 0] <- 0
  
  # Negative log-likelihood
  -sum(occ * log(J + 1e-10) + (1 - occ) * log(1 - J + 1e-10))
}

# Optimize
fit <- optim(
  par = c(e = 0.1, x = 0.5, y = 10, alpha = 0.01, b = 0.5),
  fn = IFM_fit,
  patches = patches,
  dist_matrix = dist_matrix,
  method = 'L-BFGS-B',
  lower = c(0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 0.001, 0.01),
  upper = c(10, 5, 100, 1, 3)
)

fit$par

library(EcoSimR)

cooccurrence_null_model <- function(community, n_sim = 1000) {

    pattern = if(p_value < 0.025) 'segregated' else if(p_value > 0.975) 'aggregated' else 'random')

pva_vortex_sim <- function(species_params, n_sims = 1000, n_years = 100) {
  results <- matrix(NA, nrow = n_sims, ncol = n_years)
  for (sim in 1:n_sims) {
    N <- species_params$N0
    for (t in 1:n_years) {
      ev_survival <- rnorm(1, 0, species_params$CV_survival)
      ev_fecundity <- rnorm(1, 0, species_params$CV_fecundity)
      survival <- pmin(1, pmax(0, species_params$survival + ev_survival))
      fecundity <- pmax(0, species_params$fecundity + ev_fecundity)
      catastrophe <- rbinom(1, 1, species_params$catastrophe_prob)
      if (catastrophe) {
        survival <- survival * (1 - species_params$catastrophe_severity)
        fecundity <- fecundity * (1 - species_params$catastrophe_severity)
      }
      N <- max(0, N + N * fecundity * survival - N^2 / species_params$K)
      results[sim, t] <- N
      if (N <= 0) break
    }
  }
  extinct <- apply(results, 1, function(r) sum(r > 0) < n_years)
  list(extinction_prob = mean(extinct), trajectory = results)
}

# GeoPlant benchmark evaluation
import torch
from torch.utils.data import DataLoader
import numpy as np
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score

# Spatial block CV - blocks are contiguous geographic regions
def evaluate_geoplant(model, test_loader, test_coords):
    model.eval()
    all_preds, all_labels, all_coords = [], [], []

    with torch.no_grad():
        for batch in test_loader:
            pred = model(batch['env'])
            all_preds.extend(pred.cpu().numpy())
            all_labels.extend(batch['presence'].cpu().numpy())

    # Overall AUC
    auc = roc_auc_score(all_labels, all_preds)

    # Per-block AUC (spatial extrapolation test)
    blocks = assign_spatial_blocks(test_coords, block_size_km=200)
    block_aucs = []
    for block_id in np.unique(blocks):
        mask = blocks == block_id
        if mask.sum() > 50:
            block_aucs.append(roc_auc_score(
                np.array(all_labels)[mask], np.array(all_preds)[mask]
            ))

    print(f"Overall AUC: {auc:.3f}")
    print(f"Block AUC (mean±sd): {np.mean(block_aucs):.3f}±{np.std(block_aucs):.3f}")
    return auc, block_aucs

[REASONING]
Multi-species connectivity modeling represents a significant advance over single-species corridor approaches because it identifies landscape linkages that serve multiple species simultaneously, providing more efficient conservation investments. The combination of circuit theory (which models movement as electric current flowing through a resistance surface) and least-cost path analysis (which identifies optimal routes) captures complementary aspects of connectivity: circuit theory accounts for multiple alternative pathways and the diffusion of dispersers, while least-cost paths identify the single best corridor. Expert-derived resistance surfaces for nine species with diverse ecological roles (large carnivores, small herbivores, dispersers) capture the ecological pattern that corridors must accommodate species with different movement abilities and habitat tolerances. The key assumption is that expert opinion can accurately parameterize resistance surfaces, but expert biases may systematically overestimate avoidance of certain land cover types. A limitation is that the approach assumes movement is the primary connectivity process, ignoring stepping-stone dynamics and matrix permeability variation across seasons.

import numpy as np
import networkx as nx

# Simulate multi-species corridor modeling
np.random.seed(42)

def build_resistance_layer(n=50, species='elephant'):
    # Generate species-specific resistance surface
    base = np.random.random((n, n)) * 100
    
    if species == 'elephant':
        # Wide-ranging, moderate resistance except urban
        base[base > 80] = 200  # urban = high resistance
    elif species == 'leopard':
        # Avoids open areas
        base[base < 30] = 150  # open = high resistance
    elif species == 'duiker':
        # Small antelope, sensitive to fragmentation
        base = base * 1.5
    return base

# Multi-species consensus resistance
n_species = 9
species_list = ['elephant', 'leopard', 'duiker', 'buffalo', 'bushpig', 
                'caracal', 'genet', 'mongoose', 'porcupine']
resistance_layers = np.zeros((50, 50, n_species))

for i, s in enumerate(species_list):
    resistance_layers[:,:,i] = build_resistance_layer(50, s)

# Consensus (mean resistance)
mean_resistance = np.mean(resistance_layers, axis=2)

# Least-cost path between two reserves (simplified Dijkstra)
def least_cost_path(resistance, start, end):
    nx_graph = nx.grid_2d_graph(50, 50)
    for (y, x), node in nx_graph.nodes(data=True):
        nx_graph.nodes[(y,x)]['resistance'] = resistance[y, x]
    for (y1, x1), (y2, x2) in nx_graph.edges():
        r = (resistance[y1, x1] + resistance[y2, x2]) / 2
        nx_graph[(y1,x1)][(y2,x2)]['weight'] = r
    path = nx.astar_path(nx_graph, start, end, 
                         weight='weight',
                         heuristic=lambda a,b: np.sqrt((a[0]-b[0])**2 + (a[1]-b[1])**2))
    return path

path = least_cost_path(mean_resistance, (5, 5), (45, 45))
path_cost = sum(mean_resistance[y,x] for y,x in path)
print(f"Multi-species corridor length: {len(path)} cells")
print(f"Total cost: {path_cost:.0f}")
print(f"Mean resistance along corridor: {path_cost/len(path):.1f}")

import torch
import torch.nn as nn

class MultimodalSDM(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, n_env_features, n_species, embedding_dim=64):
        super().__init__()
        self.env_encoder = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(n_env_features, 128), nn.ReLU(),
            nn.Linear(128, embedding_dim)
        )
        self.species_encoder = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(n_species, 128), nn.ReLU(),
            nn.Linear(128, embedding_dim)
        )
        self.fusion = nn.Linear(embedding_dim * 2, embedding_dim)
        self.predictor = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(embedding_dim, 64), nn.ReLU(),
            nn.Linear(64, 1)
        )
    def forward(self, env, co_occurring_species):
        env_emb = self.env_encoder(env)
        species_emb = self.species_encoder(co_occurring_species)
        fused = self.fusion(torch.cat([env_emb, species_emb], dim=-1))
        return self.predictor(fused)
```

Generalized Linear Mixed Models (GLMMs) handle hierarchical data structures common in SDM: multiple surveys per site, multiple species per survey, or nested spatial units. lme4 fits binomial GLMMs with crossed and nested random effects via Laplace approximation or adaptive Gauss-Hermite quadrature.

[CONTEXT]
Generalized Linear Mixed Models (GLMMs) handle hierarchical data structures common in SDM: multiple surveys per site, multiple species per survey, or nested spatial units. lme4 fits binomial GLMMs with crossed and nested random effects via Laplace approximation or adaptive Gauss-Hermite quadrature.

[REASONING]
STEP 1 — Hierarchical data: Species occurrence data naturally has hierarchical structure — observations nested in sites, sites in regions, regions in biomes. GLMMs model fixed effects (environment) plus random effects (site, region, observer, year). 

STEP 2 — Random effects: Random intercepts absorb variation at each hierarchical level that's not explained by fixed effects. This (a) correctly models non-independence of observations and (b) generalizes to new levels. 

STEP 3 — Crossed random effects: Observer AND site can affect detection. Crossed random effects model both simultaneously: detection ~ (1|observer) + (1|site). This handles the common situation where some observers are better at finding species and some sites are harder to survey. 

STEP 4 — Random slopes: Not just random intercepts — species may have different responses to elevation. (1 + elevation | species) fits each species its own slope. This is a simplified JSDM. 

STEP 5 — Fit via glmer: Laplace approximation is default and fast. For more accuracy, nAGQ > 0 uses adaptive quadrature (slower but handles sparse data better). PQL is fastest but biased for binomial with low counts.

[CODE]
```r
library(lme4)

# Data: multiple surveys per site
data <- read.csv('multi_survey_data.csv')

# Simple GLM (ignores hierarchy — WRONG for multi-survey data)
fit_glm <- glm(
  presence ~ bio1 + bio12 + forest_cover,
  data = data,
  family = binomial
)

# GLMM with site random effect (accounts for repeated surveys)
fit_glmm_site <- glmer(
  presence ~ bio1 + bio12 + forest_cover + (1 | site_id),
  data = data,
  family = binomial,
  nAGQ = 1  # Laplace approximation
)

# GLMM with observer AND site crossed random effects
fit_glmm_crossed <- glmer(
  presence ~ bio1 + bio12 + (1 | site_id) + (1 | observer),
  data = data,
  family = binomial
)

# Compare models
AIC(fit_glm, fit_glmm_site, fit_glmm_crossed)

# Random effects summary
ranef(fit_glmm_crossed)  # BLUPs
VarCorr(fit_glmm_crossed)  # variance components

# Site-level predictions (including random effect)
site_preds <- predict(fit_glmm_site, type = 'response',
                       re.form = ~ (1 | site_id))

# Population-level predictions (no random effects)
pop_pred <- predict(fit_glmm_site, type = 'response',
                     re.form = ~ 0)

# Random slopes: species-specific responses to elevation
fit_rs <- glmer(
  presence ~ elevation + (1 + elevation | species),
  data = multi_spp_data,
  family = binomial
)

# Species-specific elevation slopes

[REASONING]
Species context: Agaricus bisporus in Global (cultivated) (cosmopolitan). Data: eDNA water samples from 30 sites. Step 1: Obtain a high-resolution coastline shapefile for the study region and digitize islands, lakes, and peninsulas. Step 2: Construct a constrained triangular mesh where triangles crossing the barrier are removed or edges are assigned high resistance. Step 3: Define the SPDE with a barrier model that modifies the differential operator at boundaries. Step 4: The barrier effect is controlled by a parameter r: r=0 means the barrier has no effect (standard SPDE), r>0 increases resistance to spatial correlation across barriers. library(INLA)
library(INLAspacetime)

barrier_spde_sdm <- function(occ, env, coastline) {
  bnd <- inla.nonconvex.hull(as.matrix(occ[, c('lon','lat')]))
  mesh <- inla.mesh.2d(boundary = bnd, max.edge = c(0.3, 1), cutoff = 0.1)
  barrier_triangles <- inla.barrier.polygon(mesh, coastline)
  barrier_model <- inla.barrier.pcmatern(mesh, barrier.triangles = barrier_triangles,
    prior.range = c(1, 0.01), prior.sigma = c(1, 0.01))
  spde <- inla.spde2.pcmatern(mesh, prior.range = c(1, 0.01), prior.sigma = c(1, 0.01))
  A <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh, loc = as.matrix(occ[, c('lon','lat')]))
  idx <- inla.spde.make.index('spatial', n.spde = mesh$n)
  stack <- inla.stack(data = list(occ = occ$presence),
    A = list(A, 1), effects = list(spatial = idx, data.frame(intercept = 1, occ[, names(env)])))
  result <- inla(occ ~ -1 + intercept + bio1 + f(spatial, model = barrier_model),
    data = inla.stack.data(stack), family = 'binomial')
  list(mesh = mesh, barrier = barrier_model, result = result)
}
```

Step 3: Select the k most similar modern samples (typically k=5-10). Step 4: Reconstruct past climate or vegetation as the weighted average of the k analogs. Step 6: Propagate uncertainty using the standard deviation across analogs and bootstrapping.

library(rioja)

pollen_mat_reconstruction <- function(fossil_pollen, modern_pollen, modern_climate, k = 5) {
  diss <- dist(rbind(fossil_pollen, modern_pollen), method = 'sq.chord')
  diss_matrix <- as.matrix(diss)[1:nrow(fossil_pollen), -(1:nrow(fossil_pollen))]
  reconstruction <- t(apply(diss_matrix, 1, function(d) {
    analogs <- order(d)[1:k]
    weights <- 1 / d[analogs]
    weights <- weights / sum(weights)
    colSums(modern_climate[analogs, ] * weights)
  }))
  min_diss <- apply(diss_matrix, 1, min)
  reliable <- min_diss < quantile(diss_matrix, 0.05)
  list(reconstruction = reconstruction, reliable = reliable)
}
```

[REASONING]

INLA-RF's two-stage approach — INLA for the structured spatial-temporal components (trend, seasonality, spatial autocorrelation), RF for the unstructured environmental response — decomposes the prediction problem into what we can model parametrically (space and time are well-described by Gaussian processes) and what requires nonparametric flexibility (species' responses to temperature, precipitation, etc. are often multimodal, threshold-based).   f(spatial_idx, model = spde) +

train_data$residual <- train_data$occurrence - train_data$spatial_pred

  residual ~ bio1 + bio4 + bio12 + bio15 + elev + landcover,
  data = train_data, ntree = 500
)

[REASONING]
The Habitat Evaluation Procedure represents one of the earliest structured approaches to conservation planning and habitat suitability assessment, integrating multiple environmental parameters into a composite Habitat Suitability Index (HSI). This study applies HEP within a river system to identify high- and low-quality fish habitat patches, providing a quantitative basis for habitat restoration, species reproduction, and flow regulation decisions. For conservation planning, the value of HEP lies in its transparency and interpretability: each parameter's contribution to the final suitability score can be directly understood by managers. This contrasts with more complex machine learning approaches where model decisions are opaque. The identification of specific environmental thresholds (e.g., preferred depth range, velocity tolerance) makes HEP particularly useful for designing restoration actions like flow releases from dams or channel reconfiguration projects.

[CODE]

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

np.random.seed(42)
n_cells = 200

# Environmental parameters across river cells
depth = np.random.uniform(0.1, 3.0, n_cells)  # meters
velocity = np.random.uniform(0, 2.0, n_cells)  # m/s
substrate = np.random.choice(['gravel', 'sand', 'silt', 'cobble'], n_cells)
cover = np.random.uniform(0, 1, n_cells)  # proportion

# Suitability index functions (SI range 0-1)
def SI_depth(d):
    if d < 0.2: return d / 0.2
    if d < 1.0: return 1.0
    if d < 2.0: return 1.0 - (d - 1.0) / 1.0
    return 0.0

def SI_velocity(v):
    if v < 0.1: return v / 0.1
    if v < 0.6: return 1.0
    if v < 1.5: return 1.0 - (v - 0.6) / 0.9
    return 0.0

def SI_substrate(s):
    return {'gravel': 1.0, 'cobble': 0.7, 'sand': 0.4, 'silt': 0.2}[s]

def SI_cover(c):
    return min(c / 0.5, 1.0)

# Compute HSI (geometric mean)
SI_d = np.array([SI_depth(d) for d in depth])
SI_v = np.array([SI_velocity(v) for v in velocity])
SI_s = np.array([SI_substrate(s) for s in substrate])
SI_c = np.array([SI_cover(c) for c in cover])

HSI = (SI_d * SI_v * SI_s * SI_c) ** 0.25

# Classify habitat quality
quality = pd.cut(HSI, bins=[0, 0.3, 0.6, 1.0], labels=['Poor', 'Moderate', 'Good'])
print('Habitat quality distribution:')
print(pd.Series(quality).value_counts())

# Prioritize restoration cells
restoration_cells = np.where((HSI > 0.2) & (HSI < 0.5))[0]
print(f'Candidates for restoration: {len(restoration_cells)} of {n_cells}')
```

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score
from scipy.stats import logistic

# Simulate tree fern presence-only data with sampling bias
np.random.seed(42)
n = 500
# Environmental predictors: temperature and precipitation
X = np.random.uniform(0, 1, (n, 2))
# True probability of presence (logistic function)
beta = np.array([2.0, -1.5])
logit = X @ beta - 1.0
p_true = logistic.cdf(logit)
# Simulate presence-only with sampling bias: higher sampling in cluster
bias = np.exp(-((X[:,0]-0.8)**2 + (X[:,1]-0.8)**2) / 0.1)  # cluster at (0.8,0.8)
bias = bias / bias.max()
sample_prob = p_true * bias  # biased sampling
presence = np.random.binomial(1, sample_prob) > 0
# Keep only presence points (presence-only)
X_pres = X[presence]
print(f'Number of presence points: {len(X_pres)}')

# Simulate background points (10000) uniformly
n_bg = 10000
X_bg = np.random.uniform(0, 1, (n_bg, 2))

# Combine presence and background for MaxEnt-like model
X_all = np.vstack([X_pres, X_bg])
y_all = np.hstack([np.ones(len(X_pres)), np.zeros(n_bg)])

# Train logistic regression as simple MaxEnt approximation
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
model = LogisticRegression(penalty='l2', C=1e10, solver='lbfgs')
model.fit(X_all, y_all)

# Simulate independent validation presence-absence data (100 points)
X_val = np.random.uniform(0, 1, (100, 2))
logit_val = X_val @ beta - 1.0
p_val_true = logistic.cdf(logit_val)
y_val = np.random.binomial(1, p_val_true)

# Predict probabilities on validation set
pred_prob = model.predict_proba(X_val)[:, 1]
# Evaluate AUC
auc = roc_auc_score(y_val, pred_prob)
print(f'Validation AUC: {auc:.3f}')

# Simulate bias correction: use bias grid as additional predictor
# In practice, bias grid is included as a covariate
# Here we add bias as a feature
bias_val = np.exp(-((X_val[:,0]-0.8)**2 + (X_val[:,1]-0.8)**2) / 0.1)
bias_val = bias_val / bias_val.max()
X_val_bias = np.column_stack([X_val, bias_val])
# Retrain model with bias feature
X_all_bias = np.column_stack([X_all, np.exp(-((X_all[:,0]-0.8)**2 + (X_all[:,1]-0.8)**2)/0.1)])
model_bias = LogisticRegression(penalty='l2', C=1e10, solver='lbfgs')
model_bias.fit(X_all_bias, y_all)
pred_prob_bias = model_bias.predict_proba(X_val_bias)[:, 1]
auc_bias = roc_auc_score(y_val, pred_prob_bias)
print(f'Validation AUC after bias correction: {auc_bias:.3f}')

# Interpretation: AUC improves when bias is included, demonstrating importance of bias correction.

Spatial capture-recapture (SCR) estimates animal density from detections at an array of traps or camera stations. Unlike non-spatial CR, SCR explicitly models each individual's activity center as a latent spatial point, with detection probability declining with distance from this center. Enables estimation of density (N/area) without ad-hoc buffer strips.

[CONTEXT]
Spatial capture-recapture (SCR) estimates animal density from detections at an array of traps or camera stations. Unlike non-spatial CR, SCR explicitly models each individual's activity center as a latent spatial point, with detection probability declining with distance from this center. Enables estimation of density (N/area) without ad-hoc buffer strips.

[REASONING]
STEP 1 — Non-spatial CR: Estimates N (total individuals) but not area — density requires a buffer strip, which is subjective and rarely justified. SCR solves this by introducing a spatial point process for individual activity centers s_i. 

STEP 2 — Detection model: Individual i at trap j is detected with probability p_ij = p_0 × exp(-d_ij² / 2σ²), where d_ij is distance between activity center s_i and trap location x_j. p_0 = baseline detection at distance 0. σ = spatial scale of movement (home range radius). 

STEP 3 — State space: Activity centers s_i are uniformly distributed in the state space S (area buffered around traps). Density D = E[N]/|S|. The buffer must be large enough that individuals beyond S have negligible detection probability (rule: buffer > 3σ). 

STEP 4 — Likelihood: Data = detection histories y_ijk (individual i at trap j on occasion k). Parameters: D (density), p_0 (baseline detection), σ (movement scale). Estimated via MCMC (JAGS/Nimble) or maximum likelihood (secr package). 

STEP 5 — Half-normal vs exponential: Half-normal (exp(-d²/2σ²)) = circular home range with Gaussian use distribution. Exponential (exp(-d/σ)) = Laplace movement kernel. Negative exponential (1 - exp(-d/σ)) = asymptotically flat near center. 

STEP 6 — Ecological insight: Density varies with habitat via D(s) = exp(βX(s)). σ varies by sex (males typically larger). p_0 varies by survey effort (camera days).

import torch
import torch.nn as nn

class AttentionDeepMaxent(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, n_features, hidden_dim=64):
        super().__init__()
        self.attention = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(n_features, n_features),
            nn.Tanh(),
            nn.Linear(n_features, n_features),
            nn.Softmax(dim=-1)
        )
        self.mlp = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(n_features, hidden_dim),
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.Linear(hidden_dim, hidden_dim),
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.Linear(hidden_dim, 1)
        )
    
    def forward(self, x, return_attention=False):
        attn_weights = self.attention(x)
        attended = x * attn_weights
        logits = self.mlp(attended)
        if return_attention:
            return logits, attn_weights
        return logits
    
    def maxent_loss(self, presence_scores, background_scores):
        return -(presence_scores.mean() - torch.log(background_scores.exp().mean()))

functional_evenness <- function(traits, abundances) {
  dist_matrix <- dist(traits)
  mst <- spantree(dist_matrix)
  branches <- mst$dist
  weights <- abundances / sum(abundances)
  branch_weights <- (weights[mst$kid] + weights[mst$parent]) / 2
  EW <- branch_weights / sum(branch_weights)
  PEW <- EW / sum(EW)
  FEve <- sum(pmin(PEW, 1 / length(PEW)) - 1 / length(PEW)) / (1 - 1 / length(PEW))
  FEve
}
```

sdm_population_dynamics <- function(K_raster, initial_N, r = 0.5, n_years = 50, dispersal_rate = 0.1) {
  K <- K_raster[]
  K[is.na(K)] <- 0
  n_cells <- length(K)
  N <- matrix(0, nrow = n_years, ncol = n_cells)
  N[1, ] <- K / sum(K, na.rm = TRUE) * initial_N
  for (t in 2:n_years) {
    growth <- N[t-1, ] * exp(r * (1 - N[t-1, ] / pmax(K, 1)))
    dispersed <- growth * (1 - dispersal_rate)
    immigrants <- growth * dispersal_rate * 1/8
    N[t, ] <- dispersed
    for (offset in expand.grid(dr = c(-1,0,1), dc = c(-1,0,1))) {
      if (offset$dr == 0 && offset$dc == 0) next
      N[t, ] <- N[t, ] + immigrants
    }
  }
  equilibrium <- colMeans(N[25:n_years, ])
  list(trajectory = N, equilibrium = equilibrium)
}

soil_om = np.random.uniform(0.5, 5, n_sites)

habitat_occ = (habitat_prob > np.random.uniform(0.3, 0.7, n_sites)).astype(float)

rf_phyto = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=100).fit(X, phytochem_suit)

phylo_constrained_sdm <- function(occ_list, env, tree, lambda = 0.5) {
  phy_dist <- cophenetic(tree)
  phy_sim <- exp(-lambda * phy_dist / max(phy_dist))

  }
  models
}

For zero-shot species (never seen in training): use its taxonomic embedding alone — the model infers range from taxonomic position.

STEP 4 — Proximity-aware evaluation: Traditional metrics (AUC, TSS) penalize predictions equally regardless of distance. Predicting presence 10km outside the true range and 1000km outside get the same penalty. LD-SDM introduces a proximity-aware metric: error weighted by geographic distance to nearest true presence. This is ecologically meaningful — a prediction 10km off is much better than 1000km off.

STEP 5 — Key insight: Taxonomy is a proxy for ecological niche. Closely related species tend to have similar niches (phylogenetic niche conservatism). LLM embeddings capture this signal without requiring a full phylogeny. The model essentially learns: 'oaks live here, pines live there, and this new oak species probably lives near other oaks.'

import torch, torch.nn as nn
from transformers import AutoModel, AutoTokenizer

class LD_SDM(nn.Module):
    """Taxonomy-driven SDM using LLM embeddings of species names."""
    def __init__(self, llm_name="bert-base-uncased", n_location=256, hidden=256):
        super().__init__()
        self.tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(llm_name)
        self.llm = AutoModel.from_pretrained(llm_name)
        for p in self.llm.parameters():
            p.requires_grad = False  # freeze LLM weights
        
        llm_dim = self.llm.config.hidden_size
        self.species_proj = nn.Linear(llm_dim, hidden)
        self.location_encoder = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(n_location, hidden), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hidden, hidden)
        )
        self.predictor = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(hidden * 2, hidden), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hidden, 1)
        )

    def embed_species(self, name, taxonomy=None):
        """Embed species name (and optional higher taxonomy)."""
        if taxonomy:
            text = f"{name}, {taxonomy}"
        else:
            text = name
        tokens = self.tokenizer(text, return_tensors="pt", padding=True, truncation=True)
        with torch.no_grad():
            output = self.llm(**tokens)
        return output.last_hidden_state[:, 0, :]  # [CLS] token

    def forward(self, species_names, taxonomy, location_features):
        species_emb = self.embed_species(species_names, taxonomy)
        h_species = self.species_proj(species_emb)
        h_location = self.location_encoder(location_features)
        fused = torch.cat([h_species, h_location], dim=-1)
        return self.predictor(fused).squeeze(-1)

# Zero-shot prediction for an unobserved species

The paper addresses the ecological fallacy in small-area epidemiological studies of air pollution and stroke mortality. A previous study used a Poisson Bayesian hierarchical model with area-level NOx quintiles and spatial random effects, finding an association but potentially biased due to aggregating individual exposures. The ecological hypothesis is that using within-area variability in NOx exposure to estimate individual-level exposure probabilities can reduce ecological bias.
